title: Whence the sun rises
theme: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets, on which all the gods are fixed and beyond which no one goes: this is that.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «यस्मात्प्राणात्», from which prāṇa; Raṅgarāmānuja: «यस्मात् ब्रह्मण: सकाशात्», from which Brahman

the one on whom the gods are fixed (correlative of yataḥ … yatra)

words.context: Śaṅkara: Agni and the rest among the deities, speech and the rest in the body
Śaṅkara: «सम्प्रवेशिताः», made to enter; Raṅgarāmānuja: «प्रतिष्ठिताः», established

words.role: subject of atyeti; with na, ‘no one’
predicate: the Brahman Naciketas asked about

sandhi.rule: The visarga becomes s before a voiceless consonant, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः), and s becomes ś before c, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः); a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

sandhi.type: visarga before t; t before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The visarga becomes s before t, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः); a final t becomes d before a vowel, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).
Two like vowels fuse into the long vowel, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).
A final t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi_exceptions.note: The base prints sūryaḥ astam with the visarga kept and the vowels apart; the ordinary rule would give sūryo 'stam, as GRETIL, the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva's text write it (corrections.json, orthographic). Unjoined, the second pāda (astaṃ yatra ca gacchati) keeps its eight syllables.

sarve arpitāḥ: the ordinary rule would elide the a, sarve 'rpitāḥ, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति); the vishvAsa mūla writes it so. The base keeps the vowels apart, which gives the third pāda its eight syllables.

morphology.note: An accusative with arpitāḥ, ‘fixed onto him’, where a locative would be usual; both commentators explain it with a locative — Raṅgarāmānuja «तस्मिन् आत्मनि प्रतिष्ठिताः», Śaṅkara by the spokes fixed in the hub of a wheel.
ati + eti, from √i ‘go’: ‘goes beyond, passes over’. The preverb is written with the verb.
The interrogative kaḥ with the particle cana makes an indefinite, ‘anyone’; with the negative, ‘no one’.

translation.literal: From where the sun rises and where it goes to setting, on that all the gods are fixed; that indeed no one goes beyond. This truly is that.
translation.readable: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets, on which all the gods are fixed, that no one passes beyond. This is that.

anvaya: यतः च सूर्यः उदेति, यत्र च अस्तम् गच्छति, तम् सर्वे देवाः अर्पिताः [सन्ति]; तत् उ कश्चन न अत्येति । एतत् वै तत् ।
syntax: Two relative clauses (yataḥ … udeti, yatra … gacchati) are picked up by the correlative tam, on which the gods are fixed; a further clause says that no one passes beyond tat. The refrain etad vai tat closes the verse, as at 2.1.3–8.

ambiguities.topic: From what does the sun rise?
ambiguities.note: The verse names no source. Śaṅkara takes it as prāṇa, «यस्मात्प्राणात्», which is itself Brahman, «सोऽपि ब्रह्मैव»; the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.5.23) quotes the same line and says the sun rises from prāṇa. Raṅgarāmānuja takes it as Brahman directly.

Śaṅkara: no one becomes other than it, «नातीत्य तदात्मकतां तदन्यत्वं गच्छति»; Raṅgarāmānuja: no one can transgress the inner controller, as no one can step over his own shadow, «छायावत् अन्तर्यामिण: दुर्लङ्घत्वात्».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 15, 16 and 4 syllables. The first pāda (yataś codeti sūryaḥ) has seven; it has eight if sūryaḥ is read with three syllables (sū-ri-yaḥ), a resolution common in Vedic verse but marked by no witness. The unjoined hiatus sūryaḥ astam and sarve arpitāḥ keeps the second and third pādas at eight. The refrain etad vai tat (4) stands outside the metre.

beginner: The sun seems to come from somewhere every morning and go somewhere every evening. This verse says that the place it comes from and the place it returns to are the same reality the whole teaching has been pointing at. All the powers of the world, which the text calls the gods, rest on it like spokes on the hub of a wheel, and nothing can step outside it. Śaṅkara reads the source of the sun as the life-breath of the universe, and the life-breath as Brahman itself; another Upaniṣad says the sun rises from breath. Raṅgarāmānuja reads it as Brahman, the inner ruler that no one can get away from, any more than one can get away from one's own shadow. The verse ends, like those before it, with ‘this is that’: this is what Naciketas asked about.
analogy: Like the hub of a wheel: every spoke is fixed in it, and however fast the wheel turns, no spoke goes beyond it.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That from which the sun rises and into which it sets, on which all the gods are fixed, no one goes beyond. This is that — the Brahman Naciketas asked about.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara takes the source of the sun as prāṇa, «यस्मात्प्राणात्», and the gods fixed in it as the deities outside and the faculties within, «अग्न्यादयः अधिदैवं वागादयश्चाध्यात्मं», like spokes in the hub of a wheel, «अरा इव रथनाभौ». That prāṇa is itself Brahman, «सोऽपि ब्रह्मैव», and no one, going beyond it, becomes other than it: «नातीत्य तदात्मकतां तदन्यत्वं गच्छति».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For Raṅgarāmānuja the sun rises from Brahman and sets in it; the gods are established in that self, «तस्मिन् आत्मनि प्रतिष्ठिताः»; and no one can pass beyond Brahman that is the self of all, «सर्वात्मकं ब्रह्म, कोऽपि न अतिक्रमेत», because the inner controller cannot be stepped over, like one's shadow.

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: In our source Madhva's bhāṣya has no comment on this verse: the passage filed under it is his comment on 2.1.10 (it ends ॥ १० ॥ and explains ‘who sees difference here’).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base writes sūryaḥ astam and sarve arpitāḥ with the vowels apart, where the ordinary rules give sūryo 'stam and sarve 'rpitāḥ; GRETIL, the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva's text write the first joined. Apart, both pādas keep eight syllables.

advaita.text: The source of the sun is prāṇa, which is Brahman, «सोऽपि ब्रह्मैव»; nothing passes beyond it into being other than it.

visistadvaita.text: Brahman is the source and end of the sun, the ground on which the gods are established, «तस्मिन् आत्मनि प्रतिष्ठिताः», and the inner controller no one can transgress.

schools.disagreement: Both read the verse of Brahman; Śaṅkara reaches it through prāṇa and reads ‘no one goes beyond’ as ‘no one is other than it’, Raṅgarāmānuja as ‘no one escapes its rule’. Madhva's bhāṣya has no comment on the verse in our source.

parallels.note: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka quotes the same half-verse and answers it: the sun rises from prāṇa (prāṇād vā eṣa udeti), the reading Śaṅkara follows.

parallels.quote: अरा इव रथनाभौ प्राणे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितम्
parallels.note: The image Śaṅkara uses for the gods fixed in prāṇa: spokes in the hub.

contemporary.text: Sunrise and sunset are not events on the sun but on the turning earth: the sun goes nowhere. The verse, in its own way, also looks past the rising and setting to what does not move. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What in your life stays the same while everything around it rises and sets?
reflect.deeper: Why does Śaṅkara read the source of the sun as prāṇa before he calls it Brahman? What does the Bṛhadāraṇyaka parallel add?
reflect.practice: Watch a sunrise or sunset once this week, and notice what in you is watching.

flags.note: Madhva's comment filed under 2.1.9 in madhva.json is his comment on 2.1.10 (it ends ॥ १० ॥ and explains ‘who sees difference here’); it is not quoted here.
The source of the sun: prāṇa that is Brahman (Śaṅkara, with BU 1.5.23) or Brahman directly (Raṅgarāmānuja).
